title: The Stones of the Road Fill With Tenderness
text:
The stones of the road fill with tenderness

and moss; the heavens gaze sweetly

at the bluish breasts of the water that stagnates.


Brightening among puddles undone by the sun,

the bitter veins of the ferns swell with light,

spread over the cool terror of the ravine.
editorial_note: The translation keeps Urquiza's lush landscape: tender stones, stagnant water, fern veins, and ravine.

title: Your Face in Your Hair...
text:
Your face in your hair

is the pheasant in the nest;

Eros caught in the light net

of the first smile,

held still.


It is Astarte's ill-omened face

above her thighs of gold,

fearsome fruit-and magician!-

among the branches of a vague

sycamore.


It is moon in the groves

and spark upon the forge,

and, with its trembling of silks,

a handful of coins

in the water.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the luxuriant sequence of face, Eros, Astarte, moon, forge, silk, and water.

title: My Solitary and Opulent Summit
text:
My solitary and opulent summit

declined toward your shadowed valley,

which neither gold of grain nor freshness of well

nor garrulous aviary sustains.


In your gravitating, sickly light,

the balance of repose broken,

I wander over your fearful spirit

like a shred of ashen mist.


I am free to return to my hillocks

where boyish Eros plays the reed-pipe,

girdled by lambs and shepherds;


but to perpetual exile I am provoked

by the spark of your troubling eyes,

the red curling of your mouth.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sonnet's movement from pastoral freedom into chosen erotic exile.

title: A Dreaming of the Pale Branches
text:
A dreaming of the pale branches

and the plains where wheat sets,

a breathing toward solitude with you

through the damp valleys and the woodland:


a seeking of the deep and savage region,

a desire to possess you without witness,

an embraced longing to be with myself

seeing your face in an inner landscape:


such was my truest youth;

in the ideal climate of your sweetness

my divine spring matured:


and I held my hope so certain,

as though in passing beauty

your beauty gave itself to me, intact.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the sonnet's inward landscape of desire, solitude, and intact beauty.

title: Drawn by the Scent of Your Aromas...
text:
Drawn by the scent of your aromas

and drunk on the wine of your breasts,

I forgot my flock in the fallow fields

and lost my song among the apples.


As doves in flight seek

the currents rocked in their beds,

through the mountain of narrow girdles

I will seek the places where you appear.


Now across the whole earth I will go lost,

leaving the song abandoned,

the helpless herd without guard,


since I forgot my love and my dwelling,

drawn by the scent of your orchards,

drunk on the wine of your breasts.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the pastoral-erotic intoxication and the speaker's abandonment of song, flock, and home.
